posts.title: Telehandler reverse fatality: plant interface still kills when site rules are bypassed
posts.excerpt: A self-employed telehandler driver was given a suspended sentence after reversing over a lift supervisor on a Cheshire site in June 2023. The principal contractor had provided a clear turning circle; the driver still reversed without a banksman and while using a mobile phone. Workplace transport remains a major cause of construction deaths and sits at the plant–temporary works interface.
posts.linkedinReady:
A lift supervisor went to work and never came home.

On 11 June 2023 James Connolly was struck and reversed over by a telehandler on a construction site in Ince, Ellesmere Port. He was walking back from the welfare compound. Michael Nixon, a qualified and experienced telehandler operator, chose to reverse without a banksman despite a clear, unobstructed turning circle provided by the principal contractor. He was also using his mobile phone, contrary to the site rules he had signed.

At Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 11 August 2026 Nixon was sentenced to 12 weeks’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months, fined £800 and ordered to pay £2,000 costs. HSE published the prosecution on 18 August 2026.

HSE Principal Inspector Laura Royales: “Workplace transport incidents remain one of the biggest causes of deaths in the workplace. It is vital that drivers follow the site rules and do not cut corners and put lives at risk.”

For contractors and TWCs this is not only a vehicle issue. Haul roads, turning circles, pedestrian segregation and plant working platforms are temporary works territory under BS 5975 and HSE guidance. A traffic management plan that exists on paper but is ignored on the ground is not control.

Practical checks this week:
• Confirm every plant operating area has a current traffic management / segregation arrangement linked to the Temporary Works Register where relevant.
• Enforce banksman use for reversing where the site rule requires it — no exceptions for “experienced” operators.
• Zero tolerance for mobile phone use while operating plant.
• Walk the routes between welfare and workfaces; if pedestrians and reversing plant share space, redesign or control it.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On the morning of 11 June 2023, 49-year-old James Connolly was working as a lift supervisor on a large construction site in Ince, Ellesmere Port. While walking back to his work area from the welfare compound he was struck and reversed over by a telehandler operated by Michael Nixon, resulting in fatal injuries. Nixon was a self-employed, qualified and experienced telehandler operator.

The principal contractor had taken steps to minimise the need for reversing, including creation of a turning circle that was unobstructed at the time of the incident. Despite this, Nixon chose to reverse without the aid of a banksman. The investigation also found that he had been using his mobile phone while in control of the telehandler, contrary to the site rules he had signed up to.

Michael Nixon, 46, of Deeside, Heswall, Wirral, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 3(2) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. He was sentenced to 12 weeks’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, fined £800 and ordered to pay £2,000 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 11 August 2026. HSE published the prosecution on 18 August 2026.

body.h: Why this matters for temporary works control
body.p: Workplace transport remains one of the largest causes of construction fatalities. Haul roads, plant access routes, turning areas and segregation arrangements are routinely treated as temporary works items under BS 5975 management procedures and HSE guidance (including HSG144). A designed or planned traffic layout that is then bypassed by operators is a control failure of the same character as an un-designed crash deck or an un-propped excavation edge. The Temporary Works Coordinator’s role includes ensuring that plant interfaces that create temporary risk are identified, controlled and inspected.

ul: Confirm that the Temporary Works Register (or associated traffic management plan) captures plant operating areas, haul routes and pedestrian segregation where these create temporary risk.
Require and enforce banksman use for reversing wherever the site rule or risk assessment requires it — experience does not replace the control.
Treat mobile-phone use while operating plant as a serious breach; it removes the last line of awareness.
Walk the actual routes between welfare and workfaces; if pedestrians and reversing plant share uncontrolled space, redesign the layout or impose physical segregation.
Link plant working platforms, outrigger pads and edge protection of excavations adjacent to plant routes into the same temporary works procedure and permit regime.

posts.title: Premature loading of incomplete temporary works remains a recurring control failure
posts.excerpt: Recent published findings and CROSS material keep showing the same pattern: temporary formwork or platforms loaded before they are complete, inspected and permitted. Sequence changes without re-check introduce lateral-torsional and stability risks. Contractors and TWCs need the register, brief and hold points to catch this before load is applied.
posts.linkedinReady:
Premature loading of incomplete temporary works keeps appearing in published findings.

This week South Africa’s Public Works Minister released CBE investigation findings into four collapses. At the Magnolia development in Sea Point, about 40 m² of temporary formwork became unstable and failed after an incomplete and uninspected structure was prematurely loaded. Four workers were injured. The permanent structure itself did not collapse — the temporary works did.

That pattern is familiar in UK material:
• Paxton House (HSE June 2026) — timber platforms collecting concrete debris, no design, no calculated safe load, inspection not by a competent TWC.
• CROSS-UK Report 1479 (January 2026) — contractor changed the bridge-deck construction sequence; beams lifted individually instead of in pairs introduced a lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete exceeding 200% utilisation without temporary restraints.
• CROSS-UK Report 1539 (May 2026) — props designed without checking the existing RC slab and beams that had to carry the load path.

BS 5975-1:2024 management procedures exist for this. Temporary works that will carry people, debris or wet concrete belong on the register. They need a design brief that captures sequence and existing structure, a design or justified standard solution, an appropriate check, a permit-to-load, and competent inspection before load is applied.

‘We always do it this way’ or a verbal ‘don’t overload it’ is not control.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

#TemporaryWorks #BS5975 #CROSS #HSE #Formwork #ConstructionSafety #TWC

body.p: On 20 August 2026 the South African Minister of Public Works and Infrastructure released Council for the Built Environment (CBE) investigation findings into four building and structural incidents between December 2025 and March 2026. At the Magnolia residential development in Sea Point, Cape Town, on 17 February 2026, approximately 40 m² of temporary formwork at Level 3 became unstable and failed, injuring four workers. Investigators found that the permanent structure itself had not collapsed. Temporary works failed after an incomplete and uninspected structure was prematurely loaded. The site had planning approvals and appointed professionals; the failure was in construction-stage control of temporary works.

body.h: UK parallels already on the public record
body.p: The same control gap appears in UK published material. The Paxton House prosecution (HSE 15 June 2026) concerned temporary timber platforms under floor openings used to collect concrete cores and debris. There was no design, no calculation of safe load, and the person completing the inspection form was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. CROSS-UK Report 1479 (13 January 2026) recorded a contractor change to the construction sequence on a filler-beam bridge deck: beams to be lifted individually rather than in connected pairs introduced a significant temporary lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete. Without temporary restraints the utilisation exceeded 200%. CROSS-UK Report 1539 (14 May 2026) described propping for column replacement where the props themselves were adequate but the existing RC beams and slab that formed the load path had not been checked.

Temporary works reach their critical load state when wet concrete, debris, plant or people are applied. If the system is incomplete, unbraced, unrestrained or uninspected at that moment, the margin disappears. Changes to construction sequence alter the temporary stability case and must be treated as a design change requiring review, not a site preference. BS 5975-1:2024 places the Temporary Works Coordinator role at the centre of coordinating briefs, designs, checks, permits and inspections so that load is only applied after hold points are closed.

body.h: What a competent contractor and TWC should check this week
ul: Walk the live Temporary Works Register and identify every item that will carry wet concrete, debris, people or plant in the next seven days.

Confirm that each such item has a design brief capturing sequence and any existing structure, a design or justified standard solution, an appropriate check category, a permit-to-load and a recent competent inspection.
Treat any proposed change to construction sequence (beam erection order, pour sequence, prop removal) as a temporary works design change requiring review before work proceeds.
Reject ‘incomplete but we will load carefully’ — incomplete temporary works are not ready for load.
Ensure the person signing inspections is competent for the specific item, not merely available on site.

posts.title: Ad-hoc timber bracing and incomplete temporary works still put people at risk
posts.excerpt: CROSS Report 1525 highlights continued use of improvised timber bracing to masonry walls with no design, calculation or oversight. Pair that with recent HSE platform and wall cases and the picture is consistent: temporary works treated as ‘means and methods’ instead of controlled engineering.
posts.linkedinReady:
Ad-hoc temporary works still put people at risk.

CROSS-UK Report 1525 (published May 2026, still circulating) records continued use of improvised timber bracing to masonry walls — no design, no calculations, no competent oversight. The reporter had suffered a life-changing injury from a preventable masonry collapse.

The Expert Panel is clear: partially completed masonry is vulnerable to overturning from modest wind, impact or construction loads. Improvised bracing can create a false sense of security and may introduce new hazards.

Add the recent HSE picture:
• Paxton House (June 2026 fines) — timber platform loaded with concrete debris, no design, no safe load, inspection not by a competent TWC.
• Poole blockwork wall (December 2025) — backfilled before mortar had set, no temporary works design at all.

BS 5975-1:2024 is not optional paperwork. Temporary stability of walls, platforms and formwork belongs on the register, with a brief, design or justified standard solution, check, permit and competent inspection.

If your bricklaying or façade package still treats temporary restraint as ‘site means and methods’, the control gap is already open.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #BS5975 #CROSS #HSE #ConstructionSafety #TWC

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1525 (13 May 2026) concerns the continued use on sites of ad-hoc timber bracing systems supporting masonry walls. These systems lack proper temporary works design, calculations or oversight, leaving structures unstable and workers exposed. The reporter had personally suffered a life-changing injury from a preventable masonry wall collapse during construction and submitted the report to drive better practice.

body.h: Why the Expert Panel treats this as systemic
body.p: The CROSS Expert Panel notes that temporary stability of masonry walls during construction is a well-recognised safety concern. Partially completed walls can overturn under relatively modest loads such as wind, impact or construction activity. Ad-hoc or improvised bracing is sometimes used without formal design, calculation or review. While this may be an attempt to address a known risk, it may not provide reliable restraint and can introduce additional hazards because the system behaviour has not been assessed. The Panel stresses management in accordance with BS 5975 and highlights gaps that can appear in masonry packages, particularly on lower-rise projects.

body.h: The wider HSE pattern this month and earlier
body.p: Published HSE prosecutions continue to show the same control failures on platforms and walls. In June 2026 two firms were fined after a temporary wooden platform loaded with concrete debris collapsed onto a drilling operative at Paxton House in the City of London (incident February 2024). HSE found no design, no calculated safe load, and inspection not completed by a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. In December 2025 a contractor was fined £100,000 after a newly built blockwork wall, backfilled before the mortar had properly set and without any temporary works design, collapsed into an excavation and left a steel-fixer with life-changing injuries.

body.h: What a competent contractor and TWC should check this week
ul: Identify every masonry wall, freestanding panel or partially completed façade that relies on temporary restraint and ensure it is on the Temporary Works Register.
Reject improvised timber bracing that has no design, no load assessment and no competent inspection regime.

Confirm that crash decks, debris platforms and working platforms over openings or risers have a design or justified standard solution, a posted safe load and inspection by someone competent for that item.
Treat premature loading of incomplete temporary works (formwork, falsework, bracing) as a hold-point failure — not a production decision.
Ensure the design brief for propping or bracing explicitly requires assessment of the existing or permanent structure that will carry the loads.
